text: Everything in the first three lessons was setup and context. This is where you actually build a circuit, run it, and look at real output for the first time — a single qubit, one gate, and a measurement.

QuantumCircuit of 1, 1 allocates one qubit and one classical bit, where the classical bit is where the measurement result gets stored. qc.h(0) applies a Hadamard gate to qubit 0, and qc.measure(0, 0) measures qubit 0 into classical bit 0.

Before the Hadamard gate, a qubit starts in a definite state, |0>. The Hadamard gate puts it into an equal superposition of |0> and |1> — a genuine quantum state where neither outcome is determined until you measure. For this specific gate, the ideal probabilities are exact: P(0) equals 0.5 and P(1) equals 0.5, with no approximation. But that exactness is about the ideal probability — any single run of the circuit only gives you a finite sample drawn from that probability, and a finite sample practically never lands on a perfectly even split.

Qiskit's old execute convenience function has been removed. The current pattern transpiles the circuit for your chosen backend, then calls run directly on the backend. Transpile rewrites the circuit into the gate set AerSimulator expects — for a circuit this simple it's close to a no-op, but doing it unconditionally means this exact code also works unchanged against real hardware later in the course. Shots equals 1024 tells the backend to run the circuit 1024 independent times and tally the outcomes.

Running this exact code produces something like zero: 494, one: 530. Add those up and you get 1024, matching the shot count. Notice this isn't a perfect 512 and 512, even though the underlying probability is exactly 50/50. That gap is ordinary statistical shot noise from drawing a finite sample — not a bug in your circuit, and not evidence the Hadamard gate didn't work. A different random seed would give you a slightly different split again, each one a legitimate sample from that same exact distribution.
Chapter 2 starts building circuits properly, beginning with QuantumCircuit itself — the blueprint object every circuit in this course starts from.
